records.sourceFile: Personalized tendon loading reduces muscle‐tendon imbalances in male adolescent elite athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Domroes T, Weidlich K, Bohm S, Mersmann F, Arampatzis A. Personalized Tendon Loading Reduces Muscle-Tendon Imbalances in Male Adolescent Elite Athletes. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2024;34:e14555.
paper.abstract: This seasonal cohort study examined whether tendon-strain-targeted exercise changed muscle-tendon mechanical balance in adolescent elite handball athletes.
paper.tldr: Personalized tendon loading improved strength and tendon stiffness in a small adolescent handball cohort, but it did not measure fewer tendon injuries. Use it as a measured training approach, not a universal prevention prescription.
paper.methods: Thirteen male adolescent elite handball athletes added patellar-tendon exercises three times weekly for about 31 weeks, while 13 controls continued usual training. Dynamometry, ultrasonography, tendon strain, and ultrasound structural-integrity measures were assessed four times during the season.
paper.findings: Only the intervention group increased knee-extensor strength and normalized patellar-tendon stiffness. It had lower seasonal fluctuation in maximal tendon strain and descriptively fewer athletes with strain at or above 9%, while structural integrity and between-group strain changes were not significant.
paper.limitations: The small, nonrandomized male handball sample limits causal inference and transfer. Mechanical surrogate outcomes, rather than injury incidence, were measured, and the specialized imaging and strain prescription may not be routinely feasible.
paper.practicalImplications: If measurement capability is valid, individualize tendon loading and track response rather than prescribing the same relative load to every athlete. Combine training decisions with symptoms, clinical assessment, exposure, and progression tolerance.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that tendon capacity develops over time and that the same gym load can create different tissue demand across athletes. Encourage early reporting of persistent tendon symptoms rather than chasing a target strain.
paper.rtp: Use tendon loading as one part of graded capacity restoration. Return decisions still require symptoms, clinical findings, sport-specific force and speed exposure, confidence, and progression through practice.

records.sourceFile: A systematic review of the relationship between workload and injury risk of professional male soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Jiang Z, Hao Y, Jin N, Li Y. A Systematic Review of the Relationship Between Workload and Injury Risk of Professional Male Soccer Players. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2022;19:13237.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA review assessed workload and injury-risk evidence in professional male soccer through 2021.
paper.tldr: No GPS metric or ACWR threshold reliably identified a minimum injury-risk level. Workload is useful context, but availability decisions require more than one load number.
paper.methods: Two reviewers searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and SPORTDiscus through December 2021 for original English-language studies of professional male soccer players reporting load parameters and injury outcomes.
paper.findings: Short-term fixture congestion appeared to increase match-injury incidence, whereas longer congestion had no consistent overall or match-injury effect. GPS total distance, high-speed running, and acceleration had inconclusive associations; s-RPE ACWR related to non-contact injury in some studies, but no minimum-risk threshold emerged.
paper.limitations: Included studies varied in injury definitions, GPS devices, speed thresholds, analyses, and exposure windows. The evidence was observational and male professional soccer-specific, so it cannot establish causation or individual prediction.
paper.practicalImplications: Use internal and external load trends with symptoms, availability, recovery, exposure history, and schedule context. Investigate abrupt or unusual changes rather than setting one universal threshold.
paper.athleteDev: Help athletes understand why a workload score is a conversation starter, not a pass-fail injury forecast. Pair monitoring with honest reporting of recovery and emerging symptoms.
paper.rtp: Rebuild load progressively across total running, high-speed work, and sport tasks while tracking response. Avoid using ACWR or a GPS value as a standalone clearance criterion.

records.sourceFile: The effects of fixture congestion on injury in professional male soccer - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Page RM, Field A, Langley B, Harper LD, Julian R. The Effects of Fixture Congestion on Injury in Professional Male Soccer: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2023.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined injury findings when professional male soccer schedules contained at least two matches separated by four days or less.
paper.tldr: Congested schedules were usually linked with higher match-injury incidence, but the evidence cannot isolate fixture density from rotation, recovery, and other club decisions.
paper.methods: Following a preregistered PRISMA approach, the review searched four databases through February 2022 and included eight studies reporting time-loss injury data during congested professional male soccer schedules.
paper.findings: Five studies found higher match-injury incidence in congested periods. Findings for training and overall injury incidence varied, and layoff duration was typically lower during congestion.
paper.limitations: The evidence base was small and observational, with varying injury and congestion definitions. Scheduling effects could not be separated from rotation, training modification, travel, and recovery practices.
paper.practicalImplications: Plan congested weeks collaboratively: adjust exposure, recovery, rotation, and symptom surveillance while preserving the sport-specific work athletes need. Review team patterns locally.
paper.athleteDev: Frame schedule management as preparation and communication, not an assumption that every short turnaround is unsafe. Encourage prompt reporting of recovery problems during dense periods.
paper.rtp: Match return progression to current capacity and the actual fixture sequence. A short interval should increase review and coordination, not automatically determine participation.

records.sourceFile: Time loss and recurrence of lateral ligament ankle sprains in male elite soccer - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Flore Z, Hambly K, De Coninck K, Welsch G. Time-Loss and Recurrence of Lateral Ligament Ankle Sprains in Male Elite Football: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2022.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized time-loss and recurrence after lateral ligament ankle sprain in male elite soccer.
paper.tldr: Lateral ankle sprain recurrence was about 17%, while a typical absence was about 15 days but varied too much to define a reliable timeline. Time alone is a weak return guide.
paper.methods: Six databases were searched through April 2021 for English-language cohort, case, case-control, and randomized studies reporting recurrence or time-loss in male professional soccer players; 13 recurrence and 12 time-loss studies were included.
paper.findings: Among 16,442 players in the recurrence meta-analysis, recurrence was 17.11% (95% CI 13.31%-20.92%). Time-loss data were highly heterogeneous and therefore descriptive: weighted mean 15.92 days and median 14.95 days.
paper.limitations: Time-loss heterogeneity was considerable, and injury definitions, recurrence windows, severity reporting, and designs differed. Results are population estimates in male elite soccer, not individual healing or readiness criteria.
paper.practicalImplications: Use a criteria-based lateral-ankle-sprain process that includes symptoms, examination, function, sport exposure, and athlete confidence. Audit local recurrence and timelines rather than adopting the mean absence as a target.
paper.athleteDev: Clarify that early symptom improvement does not guarantee restored ankle capacity. Build confidence through progressive balance, strength, running, cutting, and ball-work exposure.
paper.rtp: Do not clear by days missed. Progress clinical, functional, and soccer-specific criteria together and monitor the response to repeated practice and match-demand tasks.

records.sourceFile: A rehabilitation algorithm after lateral ankle sprains in professional soccer - An approach based on clinical practice guidelines.pdf

paper.citation: Flore Z, Hambly K, De Coninck K, Welsch G. A Rehabilitation Algorithm After Lateral Ankle Sprains in Professional Football (Soccer): An Approach Based on Clinical Practice Guidelines. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;19(7):910-922.
paper.abstract: This clinical commentary presents a guideline-informed, criteria-based lateral-ankle-sprain rehabilitation algorithm for professional soccer.
paper.tldr: The four-level algorithm organizes symptom, clinical, functional, and kicking progression so return is not time-only. Its effectiveness and thresholds still need testing.
paper.methods: The authors integrated clinical-practice-guideline assessments, professional-soccer experience, an ankle-function score, standardized examination, functional performance tests, and interval kicking into a four-level progression model.
paper.findings: Advancement requires passing a level-dependent ankle-function score, clinical examination, and performance tests. The proposed approach links each level to expected next-stage demands and includes progressive return to ball work.
paper.limitations: This is a Level 5 clinical commentary, not an effectiveness trial. Phase-specific tests and thresholds have not been validated for sensitivity, specificity, or reinjury reduction and may not translate outside professional soccer.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the model as a transparent multidisciplinary checklist and adapt the tests to available equipment and the athlete's presentation. Record criteria and response at each progression step.
paper.athleteDev: Give athletes visible targets across symptoms, function, and soccer tasks so return is understood as rebuilding capability rather than waiting for a date.
paper.rtp: Combine algorithm steps with medical judgment, tissue healing, sport role, training response, and full-practice progression. Passing a proposed threshold alone does not prove safe return.

records.sourceFile: Acute-chronic workload ratio of professional soccer players preceding hamstring muscle injuries - A 2-season retrospective study.pdf

paper.citation: Ribeiro-Alvares JB, Cetolin T, Haupenthal A, Baroni BM. Acute-Chronic Workload Ratio of Professional Soccer Players Preceding Hamstring Muscle Injuries: A 2-Season Retrospective Study. Sport Sciences for Health. 2023.
paper.abstract: This retrospective one-team study described GPS acute:chronic workload ratios before professional male soccer hamstring injuries.
paper.tldr: Three quarters of hamstring injuries occurred without any GPS ACWR above 1.5. A danger-zone cutoff should not be the main availability decision.
paper.methods: Forty-eight professional male soccer players were reviewed across two seasons; 28 days of GPS total distance, high-speed distance, very-high-speed distance, and actions above 19 km/h were calculated before each hamstring injury.
paper.findings: Twenty players sustained hamstring injuries. Fifteen injuries had ACWR below 1.5 in all four metrics before the injurious exposure; five exceeded 1.5 for very-high-speed distance, with fewer also exceeding it for the other metrics.
paper.limitations: Only injury cases from one team were examined, without uninjured exposure controls or prospective prediction testing. Gym load was omitted, and the selected cutoff and windows may not represent total individual load.
paper.practicalImplications: Use external-load data to prompt context review, not as a binary clearance filter. Include prior injury, symptoms, sprint tolerance, clinical information, and the rest of training when planning availability.
paper.athleteDev: Avoid labeling one ratio as dangerous or safe. Teach athletes to report hamstring symptoms and recovery changes while staff progress high-speed exposure deliberately.
paper.rtp: Reintroduce high-speed running and match actions through a graded plan; do not clear or withhold an athlete solely because of an ACWR threshold.

records.sourceFile: Muscle fibre typology as a novel risk factor for hamstring strain injuries in professional soccer - A prospective cohort study.pdf

paper.citation: Lievens E, Van Vossel K, Van de Casteele F, Wezenbeek E, Deprez D, Matthys S, et al. Muscle Fibre Typology as a Novel Risk Factor for Hamstring Strain Injuries in Professional Football (Soccer): A Prospective Cohort Study. Sports Medicine. 2021.
paper.abstract: This prospective cohort study tested whether noninvasively estimated muscle-fibre typology was associated with hamstring-strain injury in professional soccer.
paper.tldr: Fast fibre typology was associated with higher hamstring-injury risk in this cohort, but it is not a deterministic, directly modifiable, or standalone screening result.
paper.methods: Professional Belgian and English soccer players were followed over three seasons. Soleus carnosine measured with proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy classified typology, and multivariable Cox models evaluated 27 index hamstring strains.
paper.findings: Fast typology was associated with 5.3-fold higher index hamstring-strain risk than slow typology in the combined cohort (95% CI 1.92-14.8). The association was reported independently in both leagues.
paper.limitations: There were relatively few injuries and the cohort was male professional soccer only. Soleus spectroscopy is a proxy for broader muscle typology, and observational association does not show that modifying training from this result prevents injury.
paper.practicalImplications: If specialist measurement is valid and feasible, consider typology as one risk-context variable alongside modifiable strength, capacity, exposure, and clinical information. Do not use it as a label or exclusion criterion.
paper.athleteDev: Communicate that biological traits are not destiny. Focus athletes on controllable preparation, recovery, honest symptom reporting, and progressive sprint exposure.
paper.rtp: Return decisions should emphasize current capacity and sport-specific tolerance. Fibre typology cannot substitute for clinical assessment, strength, high-speed exposure, and practice progression.

records.sourceFile: A musculoskeletal multifactorial individualized program for hamstring muscle injury risk reduction in professional - Results of a prospective cohort study.pdf

paper.citation: Edouard P, Lahti J, Fleres L, Ahtiainen J, Ulvila JJ, Lehtinen T, et al. A Musculoskeletal Multifactorial Individualised Programme for Hamstring Muscle Injury Risk Reduction in Professional Football: Results of a Prospective Cohort Study. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2024;10:e001866.
paper.abstract: This prospective cohort study evaluated a multifactorial, individualized hamstring-risk program in Finnish professional soccer.
paper.tldr: The program was feasible, but its primary time-to-injury comparison was not significant. Favorable secondary results should be tested locally rather than treated as proof.
paper.methods: Finnish premier-league teams used 2019 as a control season and implemented the individualized program in 2021. Screening informed lumbopelvic, range-of-motion, posterior-chain, sprint, and related training targets; Cox regression assessed hamstring injury.
paper.findings: There were 20 hamstring injuries among 90 control-season players and 16 among 87 intervention-season players. The primary hazard ratio was not significant (0.77, 95% CI 0.39-1.51); among 31 players in both seasons, secondary analysis found lower injury burden (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.53-0.85).
paper.limitations: The prior-season nonrandomized control assumes comparable seasons; COVID disruption, club implementation differences, small samples, and possible underpowering limit inference. Secondary and compliance associations cannot establish primary efficacy.
paper.practicalImplications: A multifactorial approach can organize individualized strength, sprint exposure, range of motion, lumbopelvic work, and monitoring. Define local adherence and outcome measures before assuming it reduces injuries.
paper.athleteDev: Show athletes how screening informs a flexible plan rather than a deficit label. Consistent completion and progression of relevant work may matter more than any one exercise.
paper.rtp: Use progressive capacity restoration across posterior-chain strength, sprint mechanics, running exposure, and sport practice. A program checklist does not replace tissue, symptom, and performance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Jones fractures in elite athletes—2025 international foot and ankle sports consensus and systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Balboni JM, Semelsberger SD, Boggiano VJ, Webber K, Moran J, Mast P, et al. Jones Fractures in Elite Athletes—2025 International Foot and Ankle Sports Consensus and Systematic Review. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy. 2025.
paper.abstract: This modified-Delphi consensus and systematic review addressed diagnosis and management of Jones fractures in elite athletes.
paper.tldr: Treatment and return varied by stress versus traumatic aetiology and fracture features. Imaging and specialist decision-making matter more than a fixed return-to-sport average.
paper.methods: Thirty-seven international experts completed two modified-Delphi rounds to develop 37 statements. A systematic review of 27 studies including 1,056 patients compared operative and nonoperative management in athletes.
paper.findings: Stress-aetiology fractures were treated with open reduction internal fixation in 86.4% of cases, with mean return at 13.3 plus or minus 4.5 weeks and 8.4% complications. Traumatic fractures returned at 11.6 plus or minus 2.2 weeks regardless of modality; treatment failure was highest for conservatively managed traumatic fractures (16.1%).
paper.limitations: This is Level V consensus supported largely by nonrandomized studies with varying treatment selection, chronicity, athlete level, and return criteria. Some statements lacked clinical data, and expert consensus cannot eliminate bias.
paper.practicalImplications: Differentiate stress and traumatic presentation, use appropriate imaging, and coordinate orthopedic, rehabilitation, and performance decisions. Discuss timelines as ranges tied to healing and sport demand.
paper.athleteDev: Explain why a Jones fracture needs individualized imaging and progression rather than comparison with another athlete's timeline. Emphasize adherence to loading and healing restrictions.
paper.rtp: Confirm healing and functional sport demands before return. Surgical status or an average return time alone cannot establish readiness for practice or competition.

records.sourceFile: Evidence-based hamstring injury prevention and risk factor management - A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.pdf

paper.citation: Rudisill SS, Varady NH, Kucharik MP, Eberlin CT, Martin SD. Evidence-Based Hamstring Injury Prevention and Risk Factor Management: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized randomized trials of hamstring-injury prevention and modifiable risk-factor interventions in adult sport participants.
paper.tldr: Eccentric training reduced hamstring-injury incidence and improved several related capacities, but the evidence does not specify one optimal exercise, dose, or individual solution.
paper.methods: MEDLINE, CINAHL, Cochrane Central, and SPORTDiscus were searched in October 2020. One hundred eight parallel-group randomized trials in noninjured adult recreational, semiprofessional, or professional athletes were included.
paper.findings: Eccentric training reduced injury incidence by 56.8%-70.0% and improved concentric strength, eccentric strength, fascicle length, functional hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio, and strength asymmetry. Static stretching produced the largest flexibility gains but with more transient effects than other approaches.
paper.limitations: Nineteen trials had some risk-of-bias concerns and seven were high risk, often from randomization or missing data; blinding was usually impossible. English-only searching and heterogeneous interventions, outcomes, and populations limited pooling and protocol certainty.
paper.practicalImplications: Include progressive eccentric hamstring loading within a broader preparation plan, then select flexibility, strength, sprint, and sport-specific work according to the athlete's needs and response.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes that prevention is repeated capacity building, not a one-time exercise. Progress effort and range carefully, and communicate soreness or symptoms that change normal training response.
paper.rtp: Use eccentric work to rebuild capacity when appropriate, then demonstrate transfer through high-speed running, acceleration, deceleration, and sport-specific exposure. No isolated strength or flexibility result is return clearance.
